templates.text: Visual tracking is inconsistent, with gaze often slipping from a moving object.
The newborn's visual fixation is brief, breaking after only {seconds} seconds of focus.
A mild delay in visual orientation to a nearby face is noted.
Visual attention is easily disrupted by minor auditory or tactile stimuli.
Pupillary response to light is present but sluggish in its constriction.
The infant's visual field seems narrowed, with peripheral stimuli often missed.
Visual following is jerky and loses smooth pursuit over short distances.
There is a subtle lag in turning the head toward a novel visual target.
Contrast sensitivity appears reduced, making low-contrast patterns hard to discern.
Visual alertness cycles quickly, with periods of bright-eyed looking followed by rapid disengagement.
The baby's cry intensity does not modulate in response to visual cues from the caregiver.
Fixation on a human face is achieved but not sustained, drifting away prematurely.
Visual-motor coordination is immature, with reaching gestures poorly aligned to seen objects.
The infant startles to sound but shows a dampened visual orienting reflex to the same stimulus.
Acuity is developing, resulting in a fuzzy perception of fine details.
Visual exploration of the environment is limited to high-contrast edges within a close range.
The newborn squints or blinks excessively under normal ambient lighting conditions.
Convergence of the eyes is unsteady when attempting to focus on a near object.
A patterned visual stimulus elicits less quieting and sustained attention than expected.
The visual system is easily overwhelmed, leading to gaze aversion after brief periods of input.
Tracking a red ring is initiated but falters, requiring the object to be moved very slowly.
Depth perception cues are poorly integrated, affecting the accuracy of visual-guided movements.
The infant shows a preference for auditory soothing over visual engagement for regulation.
Visual recognition of a repeatedly shown object shows minimal habituation.
The corneal reflex is intact, but the blink response to a visual threat is slightly delayed.
Pupils show a mild anisocoria that varies, suggesting immature neural visual pathways.
Visual interest is fleeting, shifting from one target to another without deep processing.
The baby's eyes rove slowly when at rest, lacking the sharp, purposeful saccades of full-term infants.
Optokinetic nystagmus can be elicited but is irregular and unsustained.
Visual processing is inefficient, requiring longer latency to recognize a familiar face.
